extracted.intended_audience: comedians, comedy venue organizers, philosophers and ethicists of humour, and scholars/practitioners interested in ethics of offensive comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance on when offensive jokes are ethically permissible or off-limits in comedic performance, with emphasis on what jokes do, audience uptake, and contextual harms rather than only on targets or intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't punch down ethic
rubrics_metrics.description: An ethic adopted by some comedy nights/venues that rules out jokes that target the disadvantaged, vulnerable, and oppressed — i.e., 'don't punch down'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a straightforward rule of thumb that many venues follow to bar racist, homophobic, sexist, transphobic, ableist humour and other jokes aimed at marginalised groups. The author argues it is attractive but ultimately misdirects attention by emphasising relative standing of joker and target and the ostensible target rather than the joke's effects and audience. It can both rule out too much and too little (e.g., idiosyncratic nasty jokes that don't tie to background stereotypes, or punching-up jokes that nevertheless reinforce norms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate what a joke does (effects-focused criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess jokes by what they do: whether, and how, an offensive joke contributes towards undermining anti-discriminatory norms, or towards reinforcing unjust hierarchies and damaging stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift attention from the comedian's position or stated intent to the expected or likely effects of the joke in its context; consider whether the joke provides support to underlying discriminatory beliefs by reminding an audience of stereotypes or diminishing perceived seriousness of harms (e.g., rape jokes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience uptake and reception
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience's interpretation and reaction is a crucial, often determining, factor in ethical assessments of jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joke intended as subversive can fail if the audience interprets it as endorsing discriminatory attitudes; the comedian must consider both the immediate room and potential downstream audiences (clips/shared content). The audience's laughter often signals acceptability, making the public endorsement aspect ethically relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance vs. subversion of discriminatory beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish jokes that rely on discriminatory beliefs or stereotypes without subverting them from those that aim to subvert or expose such beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes that rely on background stereotypes but do not subvert them are more likely to 'punch' (harm). Subversive jokes that challenge stereotypes may still rely on them but can be ethically different — provided audience uptake recognizes the subversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedian's relative standing and identity disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of the comedian's social identity and relative standing vis-à-vis the joked-about party as influencing how a joke is received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedians often set up material to signal they have the standing to tell certain jokes; knowledge of the comedian's identity can change perception. However, standing alone does not determine whether a joke does harm; it's only one contextual factor and can mislead if overemphasised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent and avoidability of exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether audience members consented or could reasonably avoid exposure to the offensive material affects the ethical assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attending a comedy performance typically implies consenting to possible offence and weakens complaints (per Feinberg-style avoidability argument). Mixed bills, surprise performers, and variable advance notice complicate the consent assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public nature, scale and spread (stage vs. internet)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public and often large-scale dissemination of comedic performances — including clips online — amplifies risks because jokes can reach audiences beyond the intended room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joke's downstream audience (social media, clips) may misinterpret it; comedians must consider broader potential audiences in the internet era. The larger/spread the audience, the greater the potential contribution to background injustices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jokes demand assent (laughter) and create social pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy tends to solicit active assent (laughs) from audiences, which can function as a public signal of acceptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because comedians structure shows to elicit laughs and because social pressure to laugh exists, audience laughter can publicly endorse the joke's content and thereby help normalize harmful attitudes. The performative, expectant nature of comedy amplifies ethical stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution to background injustices ('support' criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A discriminatory offensive joke is problematic when it provides support to underlying discriminatory beliefs by likely reinforcing stereotypes or diminishing the perceived seriousness of harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should focus on the likely or reasonably anticipated effect on background beliefs and attitudes (not merely intent). Even small, distributed contributions can matter because comedians have a public platform; these increments can circulate and perpetuate stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idiosyncratic nasty jokes (contextual relevance of stereotype)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that target a marginalised person or group in an idiosyncratic way that does not connect to widely shared background tropes may 'punch down' yet not contribute to structural discriminatory harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'don't be mean' reading of don't punch down would rule these out, but the effects-focused approach may deem them less harmful if they don't tap into shared stereotypes or reinforce unjust norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punching up can still affirm discriminatory norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Offensive jokes that target powerful figures (punching up) may still draw on or affirm sexist, ableist, anti-fat, or other discriminatory norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume punching up is automatically harmless; consider whether the joke's content reaffirms harmful stereotypes or social norms even while targeting the powerful (e.g., mocking a politician's appearance via sexist beauty norms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failed subversive jokes (risk of misfire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subversive jokes that intend to challenge stereotypes can fail if the audience laughs at the discriminatory content rather than the target of critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure can occur in-room or later when clips are shared; if the audience 'gets it wrong', the joke may have the same harmful effect as a punching-down joke. Comedians should assess audience likelihood of understanding subversion before telling risky material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nuance over target and intent: focus on context
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid relying solely on the ostensible target or the comedian's intent; instead attend to context, background norms, and likely reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ethic of don't punch down encourages focusing on the target/intent, but this can mislead. Better ethical deliberation examines what the joke does in its specific context — which stereotypes it invokes, how fragile the anti-discriminatory norm is, and how the audience will receive it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedian's duty to prepare and read the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians bear responsibility not only for telling jokes but for preparing audiences so jokes are received as intended (e.g., set-up, signalling standing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comedian who tells risky material to an audience likely to misinterpret it shares blame (analogy: leaving a child in a room with sweets). Good comedians are expected to be skilled at reading audiences and framing material appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing comedy's social value against harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider comedy's societal roles — subversion, freedom to play with ideas, criticism of power — when weighing whether an offensive joke is permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While comedy has valuable functions (artistic critique, protest, benign violation), these do not automatically outweigh harms such as contributing to oppression; not all offensive jokes are justified by freedom-of-expression or artistic value. The author rejects a simple consequentialist calculus that treats small pleasures as outweighing oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who counts as the relevant audience (local vs distant audiences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which audiences matter for ethical assessment: the immediate live audience, the likely online viewers, or all potential downstream audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the same joke can be consumed differently across audiences and contexts, comedians must ask 'Who is the audience?' — a particularly difficult question in the internet era. Avoiding any possible misinterpretation would rule out too much, but ignoring broader audiences is naïve.
